title: Responsive Forms and Controls knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Responsive Forms and Controls”?
questions.explanation: The source curriculum lists “Flexible form layouts” under “Responsive Forms and Controls”. The lesson applies this syllabus point to a small CSS example and a browser check.

questions.prompt: Which practice best supports reliable work with responsive forms and controls?
options: Start with a fluid base layout and add a breakpoint only when the content needs a different arrangement.
Add !important to every declaration so conflicts disappear.
Assume the newest CSS feature behaves identically in all browsers.
Remove focus styles because a mouse user can see the hovered element.
questions.answer_key: Start with a fluid base layout and add a breakpoint only when the content needs a different arrangement.
questions.explanation: The key practice is: Start with a fluid base layout and add a breakpoint only when the content needs a different arrangement. For advanced features, inspect the relevant documentation and target-browser compatibility.

questions.prompt: If an example related to “Responsive Forms and Controls” does not look or behave as expected, what is the strongest first response?
options: Inspect the matched and computed styles, change one cause, and retest the original scenario.
Add several unrelated overrides until the screenshot looks closer.
Only check the default viewport and skip interactive states.
Treat an unused declaration as proof that the browser is broken.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the matched and computed styles, change one cause, and retest the original scenario.
questions.explanation: A repeatable inspection loop is more reliable than layering on overrides: inspect what matched, identify the computed value, change one cause, and retest.
